text: Numbers like the mean and standard deviation compress a whole dataset into a few values. A chart shows you everything at once: skew, peaks, gaps, and outliers. This lesson wraps up Chapter 1 with the workhorse charts for a numeric variable.

A histogram divides values into bins and shows the count in each, so it shows shape directly. A box plot shows the median, the middle half of the data, and flagged outliers, and it's great for comparing groups. A density plot is a smoothed histogram. And for a categorical variable, use a bar chart of counts.
Here's one figure with all three views of the same illustrative right-skewed order values. Matplotlib does the histogram with thirty bins and the box plot, and pandas draws the density curve.

Here is the output of that code. The histogram shows a tall spike near zero and a long right tail. The box plot shows the median well left of center, and a long trail of flagged points. And notice an honest flaw in the density plot: the curve leaks below zero, even though no order can be negative. Smoothing doesn't know your data's limits.

Box plots flag points beyond one and a half times the IQR above the third quartile. Computing that fence ourselves gives eighty-seven point eight two, and two hundred eighty-three of five thousand values lie above it. For skewed data, that rule flags plenty of legitimate large values. Treat it as a flag to investigate, never a reason to delete.

Some cautions. Bin width changes the story: three bins hide the shape, three hundred look jagged, so try several. Smoothing can spill past real limits. Outlier flags are a reason to look, not delete. And always label axes and units.
That completes descriptive statistics. Next, in lesson 7, we begin Chapter 2 with the foundation of everything ahead: probability basics.
